title: Autistic children and adolescents have difficulty perceiving speech in social and non-social noise
description: Difficulty perceiving speech in noisy environments is common in autistic individuals and may be associated with an attentional bias toward non-social stimuli. Our previous study found no interactive effect of social and non-social noise on the relationship between autistic traits and difficulties perceiving speech in noise. However, this effect may be observed in autistic children and adolescents, who have a greater attentional bias than individuals with high autistic traits in the general population. In this context, this study tested two hypotheses: (1) autistic children and adolescents show greater difficulty perceiving speech in noisy environments than their non-autistic peers, and (2) they experience greater difficulty perceiving speech in non-vocal noise than in vocal noise. Participants detected words embedded in vocal and non-vocal background noise. Autistic participants had greater difficulty with speech perception in noisy environments than their non-autistic peers, thus supporting the first hypothesis. This difference is not explained by speech perception in silence or by a preference for noise. Our second hypothesis was not supported, which is consistent with the results of our previous study. Autistic children experienced difficulty perceiving speech in both vocal and non-vocal noise. These results suggest that difficulty perceiving speech in noise may be explained by autistic traits other than an attentional bias toward non-vocal sounds.

title: Future-oriented action interventions promote personal and civic climate action
description: A majority of people are concerned about climate change but under-engaged in climate action, especially civic or collective action. We integrated insights from multiple traditions of future-oriented psychological interventions focused on imagination and action planning, and we tested the resulting psychological intervention through three experimental conditions that targeted either a personal (e.g., driving less) or civic climate action (e.g., contacting elected officials about climate change), or neither. Participants then reported their intention to engage in personal and civic pro-environmental behaviors. Preregistered analyses (on N = 1,586 participants) showed that both personal and civic action interventions increased the targeted pro-environmental behavior. Furthermore, these effects extended to other other (non-targeted) pro-environmental behaviors, though only to the same category of action (personal vs. civic). In a second preregistered study, we replicated the intention effects of the civic action intervention. This study extends prior theory about the psychology of behavior change and provides practical insights to bridge the gap between climate concern and engagement in coordinated climate initiatives.

title: Visuospatial features influencing the evaluation of two-body interactions
description: Visual evaluation of aesthetic, semantic, and emotional aspects of two-body interactions is fundamental for social cognition, yet the contribution of objective stimulus features to these evaluations remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how different visuospatial features of two-body implied interactions influence their evaluations in terms of aesthetic pleasure, symmetry, emotional valence, meaning, and interest. Across four studies involving 200 participants, we found that visually ‘entangled’ two-body interactions, defined by the extent of shared interpersonal space, were rated as more aesthetically pleasing, interesting, and meaningful than their disentangled versions. Using Representational Similarity Analysis and hierarchical multiple regressions, we identified the contribution of each stimulus feature to these evaluations. These findings suggest that two-body entanglement enhances the perceived dyads’ aesthetic and semantic value, possibly facilitating their configural processing. The study expands prior literature and highlights a dissociation between visuospatial features and mechanisms underlying pleasure and interest in dancing bodies.

title: Linguistic diversity as a two-step process: Grounding polysemy in universal neural networks and expanding it by cultural learning
description:
This paper advances a new account of linguistic typology grounded in the hypothesis of neural reuse, namely that languages selectively recruit pre-existing neurocognitive systems for grammatical purposes. The proposal is tested through a case study of the Mandarin classifier zuò (座), combining cognitive semantic analysis with fMRI evidence. The semantic analysis shows that zuò forms a highly structured polysemy network organized around scene-based construal, progressing from anchored entities and perceptual salience to bounded environments, landmarks, navigable spaces, and goal-directed schemas.
To examine whether this organization reflects underlying neural systems, an fMRI experiment contrasted zuò with a non-scene classifier. Processing zuò alone—prior to any scene-denoting noun—activated regions associated with scene perception and navigation, including the parahippocampal place area, retrosplenial cortex, and occipital place area. This indicates that a grammatical morpheme can recruit a scene-selective cortical system, supporting the view that polysemy may be constrained by shared neural architecture.
At the same time, the full semantic range of the classifier cannot be derived from neural structure alone. Several extensions depend on lived experience and culture-specific knowledge, suggesting that neural reuse provides a scaffold that is subsequently elaborated through usage and cultural models. The findings support a typological perspective in which languages differ in whether and how they recruit available neural systems, thereby shaping the emergence of grammatical categories and polysemy networks.

title: Self-regulation shapes who benefits from large language models
description: Large language models (LLMs) promise to broaden access to expertise, yet their benefits are uneven: the same model can scaffold a novice, accelerate an expert, or produce polished work that masks shallow understanding. We apply the established framework of self-regulated learning to human–LLM interaction and argue that loop quality emerges from the user–task–interface system rather than residing in the user alone. Productive loops involve three observable moves: steering sets goals and standards; monitoring evaluates fluent but fallible output; and repair tests, critiques, and revises it. Weak loops can create a synthesis trap in which users offload comparison and integration, producing false mastery—better assisted performance without corresponding transfer, confidence calibration, or error detection—and accumulating verification debt. The framework predicts that LLMs will widen differences between users when verification burden is high and regulatory support is weak, but narrow them when tasks are verifiable and interfaces externalize standards, evidence, and checks. We propose constraint density, monitoring calibration, and repair depth as process markers linking interaction traces to independent outcomes. This account turns divergent findings into testable predictions and motivates cognitive workbenches designed to preserve verification, agency, and transfer.

title: The Saito Loop, a computational theory of hierarchical recovery in catatonia
description: Clinical observation identified a reproducible recovery hierarchy in catatonia, the Saito Loop (πs → β → πm → πv_fast → πv_slow), but not why recovery should follow any fixed order. We ask whether the order follows from an active-inference architecture without being supplied. The five computational quantities follow a priori from their computational roles; structural identifiability analysis then reconstructs their prerequisite relations as a directed acyclic graph. Because the graph is a chain, its topological ordering is unique and identical to the Saito Loop: the order is a structural consequence of the dependency relations, not a fitted sequence, and the complete ordering is never supplied. All uniqueness claims hold within an explicitly specified model class, and whether the structural order is realized in recovery time is a separate, falsifiable dynamical question. The clinically observed recovery hierarchy therefore becomes a constrained computational consequence rather than an empirical regularity.

title: Pupil Dynamics Are Associated with Individual Differences in Visual Time-Reproduction Accuracy
description: Accurate temporal reproduction depends on the interaction between sensory encoding, attention, motor production, and bodily state. Visual timing is especially likely to be influenced by oculomotor behavior because the eyes continuously stabilize, interrupt, and resample visual input through pupil-linked arousal changes. The present study tested whether spontaneous pupil fluctuations track moment-to-moment timing or stable individual differences. Eighty healthy adults reproduced visually presented intervals at a fixed viewing distance of 120 cm while pupil size was recorded continuously at 500 Hz. After preprocessing, 4,104 valid participant-trials were available. The primary outcomes were signed relative reproduction error, indexing directional bias, and absolute error, indexing timing precision. Mixed-effects models and participant-level regressions were used to examine within-participant and between-participant associations. Pupil metrics showed weaker trial-level effects, but reduced participant-level pupil models predicted both signed bias and absolute error, suggesting that stable pupil-linked arousal profiles relate to individual timing precision. These findings suggest that the eyes do not merely record visual time-varying events; their stabilization, interruption, and arousal-linked dynamics are embedded in how visual durations are reproduced.

title: The Impact of Complexity on Risky Choices: An Evidence Accumulation Account
description:
Risky options often differ not only in outcomes and probabilities, but also in the cognitive demands required to evaluate them. Yet most theories of risky choice either ignore complexity or treat it as a static feature of the option, modeled as a utility discount or with heteroscedastic errors. We propose a process-level framework that explains how complexity shapes both choice and response time within an evidence-accumulation architecture. The framework assumes that complexity reduces the signal-to-noise ratio of evidence accumulation, making evaluation slower and choices less consistent, and that decision makers partly adapt to these processing constraints by adjusting their decision strategies. These mechanisms can explain how complexity reduces choice consistency and how it shifts preferences toward simpler options.
We evaluated this framework in three preregistered experiments that manipulated complexity in structurally distinct ways: through the number of outcomes, arithmetic expressions of outcomes, and compound probabilities. Across studies, complexity made choices slower and less consistent. When both options were complex, these effects were best explained by reduced signal-to-noise ratios and partially compensatory increases in decision thresholds. When options differed in complexity, preferences for simpler options were best explained by an initial bias toward simplicity combined with a drift-rate adjustment during accumulation. The compound-probability manipulation, however, marked a boundary condition: different forms of complexity can change the representations that evidence accumulation operates on. Together, these findings advance a dynamic account of risky choice in which complexity shapes preference construction by changing both the rate at which decision evidence accumulates and the strategies used to evaluate the options.

title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
description: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

title: Sparse Residual Estimation in Partially Confirmatory Factor Analysis
description:
This article extends the Bayesian regularized variational procedure for partially confirmatory factor analysis to accommodate sparse residual dependence. Existing PCFA-VA assumes a diagonal residual covariance, which may be restrictive in practice. Using continuous spike-and-slab priors, the proposed method jointly selects factor loadings and residual dependence structures while allowing available expert knowledge to be incorporated. It spans a broad confirmatory-exploratory continuum, accommodating fully or partially specified loading structures with residual dependence selection and fully unspecified loading structures with partially specified residual dependence. Rather than relying on stochastic posterior sampling, we develop a variational expectation conditional maximization (VECM) algorithm for posterior approximation and estimation. By varying the scale of the spike densities along a regularization path, the algorithm supports dynamic model exploration and progressively removes negligible loadings and residual dependence relations. Simulations demonstrate the framework's flexibility under diagonal and non-diagonal residual structures. When residual dependence is absent, it retains PCFA-VA as a special case and yields lower estimation error. When residual dependence is present, it achieves structure recovery and estimation accuracy comparable to the MCMC-based PCFA method, at markedly lower computational cost. An empirical application further illustrates that the loading and residual dependence structures selected by VECM are substantively interpretable. }

title: Seeing the world through others' minds: Determining the role of executive functions in social cognitive processes
description: Our ability to infer others’ mental states (e.g., perspectives and beliefs) is integral to successful social interaction. A long-standing debate is whether mentalising relies upon specialised social-cognitive processes or more domain-general systems that coordinate our thoughts and behaviour across social and non-social contexts. In this preregistered study, we investigated this directly by determining the causal links between mentalising and three supposedly distinct domain-general executive functions (EFs): interference resolution (the suppression of task-irrelevant information), set shifting (the flexible switching between cognitive states) and memory updating (using new information to update memory representations). A large sample (N=369) completed an online battery of three experimental tasks that measured each of the EFs and a fourth that measured mentalising – our ability to infer how the world appears from someone’s else viewpoint (level-2 visuospatial perspective-taking; VPT-2) and acknowledge that others’ belief about the world may align with or diverge from our privileged knowledge of reality (true- and false-belief reasoning). Two structural equation models were applied to data acquired with this battery to evaluate direct and indirect pathways between EFs and mentalising. Contrary to our hypotheses, these models suggest that better memory updating  and interference resolution increased the cognitive costs associated with VPT-2 and false-belief reasoning, respectively, while set shifting showed no significant effects on mentalising. Furthermore, VPT-2 did not mediate any of the causal pathways between EFs and belief reasoning. This study indicates that EFs contribute to mentalising in subtle and complex ways, and our experimental rigour reveals several methodological considerations for future research.

title: Human-Supervised LLM-Assisted Mapping of Educational Research at Scale: A Mathematics Education Demonstration
description: Large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for large-scale research synthesis, but their use in educational content analysis requires workflows that are reliable, auditable, and researcher-defined. This study develops and evaluates a human-supervised, multi-model LLM workflow for educational research mapping. Using mathematics education as a demonstration field, we annotated 4,940 abstracts published between 2001 and 2025. We developed and pilot-calibrated a hierarchical five-module coding framework before applying it to the full corpus. The framework coded each article’s analytic focus, whether mathematical content or processes (MCP) were foregrounded, research method, and sociocultural or individual-characteristic labels (ISC); for records coded as empirical and MCP-present, it also coded the primary mathematical area or practice. Two primary LLMs independently applied the framework; a third model addressed disagreement cases, followed by human audit and adjudication. Agreement between the two primary LLMs was strong across major modules (κ = .748 - .892). Human audit showed high alignment for model-agreed cases (κ = .777 - .974), whereas cases requiring auxiliary-model majority resolution showed lower and more variable agreement with human labels (κ = .600 - .791). Thus, model disagreement identified boundary cases requiring human review. The final labels supported descriptive field mapping: educator-focused research became the largest analytic-focus category, attention to sociocultural and individual characteristics increased, and overlap between empirical mathematics-focused work and ISC-coded work remained limited. LLM-assisted research synthesis is most trustworthy when implemented as an auditable workflow rather than as a one-step classification procedure.

title: AI-Faces by Illinois: A Database of AI-Generated Faces Depicting Children
description: Faces serve as gateways of impression formation during human interactions and are widely used as stimuli throughout psychological research. To source these stimuli, researchers often rely on established databases of photographs of adults’ and children’s faces or public image repositories like Google Images. Although these resources have proven valuable, there are important limitations, especially for research using images of children. This manuscript introduces a novel alternative to those databases: AI-Faces by Illinois, a database of 1,152 photorealistic, AI-generated images depicting child faces that is freely available for non-commercial use (OSF link to images and norming data: https://osf.io/vurm5/; CC-BY-NC-4.0 license). These images vary systematically by perceived age (3, 6, 10, 15 years), gender (boy, girl), race/ethnicity (Black, East Asian, Latine, Middle Eastern/North African, Native American, Pacific Islander, South Asian, White), and emotional expression (10 smiling, 4 angry, 4 frowning images per group). Two norming studies (Study 1: N = 1,261, Study 2: N = 131) revealed that adults rated the AI-generated images as equally real as the photographs of children from existing databases and perceived them in line with their prompted age, gender, race/ethnicity, and emotion. The images also elicited perceptual biases similar to those documented in research using real faces, supporting their ecological validity. This manuscript highlights the methodological advantages and new ethical considerations of using AI-generated faces of children in psychological research.

title: Friends and strangers engage in distinct regimes of body motion synchrony during conversation
description: When people talk, their bodies often move together, usually unnoticed. Researchers have studied this synchrony as one behavior. We show that it is several, and that they resolve into two distinct regimes: one for friends and one for strangers. To do so, we analyzed 387 conversations between friends and strangers using markerless pose estimation. We identify three separable forms of body motion synchrony (quantity, directional, and pseudo-synchrony) and largely explain them through four mechanisms (turn-taking, conservation of motion, entrainment, and station keeping). Both the forms and mechanisms of synchrony differ between friends and strangers. Friends synchronize in strong, simple way, moving as a single embodied system (“co-enaction"). Strangers synchronize in a more heterogenous regime, navigating a set of norms (“regulation”). These findings suggest that body motion synchrony is best understood not as single behavior but as paralinguistic scaffolding, its form shaped by the conversation – and relationship – it supports.

title: Open science in a contentious field: How transparent is research on social media and adolescent mental health?
description: The impact of social media on adolescent mental health is a topic of heated debate. In contexts such as these, where evidence is contested and policy stakes are high, research transparency is especially important. Transparent research practices facilitate independent scrutiny and informed decision-making. The present study aimed to assess the adoption of transparent research practices in studies investigating the impact of social media on adolescent mental health. A corpus of 235 eligible empirical articles was identified via a collaborative review maintained by prominent researchers in the field. Articles were coded for eight transparency indicators. Results indicated that while open access, funding statements and conflict of interest statements were relatively common (≥74%), preregistration, data sharing, materials sharing, analysis script sharing, and use of reporting guidelines were rare (≤14%). This widespread lack of transparency undermines the credibility of evidence in this contentious policy-relevant domain.

title: Measuring U.S. and Kenyan children’s vocabularies using object, photograph, cartoon, and line drawing stimuli
description: Early childhood assessments typically involve picture stimuli. As these assessments spread worldwide, researchers make an implicit assumption: that children across contexts understand pictures in the same way, at the same developmental timepoint. What if this assumption does not hold for some or all kinds of pictures? In the present research, preregistered samples of 128 3- to 7-year-olds from Kisumu, Kenya (Experiment 1) and 64 3- to 4-year-olds from the San Francisco Bay Area, U.S.A. (Experiment 2) participated in a vocabulary assessment in four formats (i.e., objects, photographs, cartoons, black-and-white line drawings). Preregistered analyses showed that children from both contexts performed similarly across object, photograph, and cartoon formats, though additional exploratory analyses suggested that Kisumu children may perform less accurately in the line drawing format, at least for ambiguous stimuli. Moreover, exploratory error analyses revealed that the children from Kisumu made different kinds of errors in the object format than in the picture formats, whereas the children from the San Francisco Bay Area made more similar kinds of errors across object and picture formats. These findings tentatively bring more confidence to the existing use of photograph- and cartoon-based assessments in global contexts, though more research is necessary to replicate the current findings, and to determine in exactly which contexts picture-based assessments are appropriate or inappropriate.

title: Inconclusive prospective effects between problematic social media use and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms: A comment on Nagata et al. (2026)
description: In a recent study, Nagata et al. concluded prospective within-individual associations between problematic social media use (PSMU) and ADHD symptoms. In the present reanalyses, we report discrepant increasing and decreasing effects of PSMU on subsequent change in ADHD symptoms, and vice versa, depending on the model used to analyze data. Meta-analytic aggregations of these divergent effects did not differ significantly from zero. Hence, we conclude that the findings by Nagata et al. may have been spurious and their conclusions premature. It is important to bear in mind that correlations, including cross-lagged effects, in observational data may be spurious in order not to overinterpret findings. For increased analytic rigor, we recommend researchers to fit, as we did here, alternative models to data to verify whether results are robust under different justifiable analytical strategies.

title: Very little data tampering is needed to produce statistically significant results: A Monte Carlo simulation
description: Simulation studies to date have examined the impact of Questionable Research Practices on the false positive rate of common statistical inference tests (e.g., Stefan & Schonbrödt, 2023), but not the impact of unquestionably undesirable research practices, such as fabrication and falsification. While any result can be obtained through sufficient fabrication or falsification, we have little insight into how much of either is needed to generate statistically significant results under a null hypothesis. This article therefore simulates data generated under the true null hypothesis and alters, deletes, or invents one data point at a time, targeting the data points that most oppose the desired result, and re-running the test after every change until it is significant in the intended direction. Six tampering strategies (dropping cases, switching condition labels, re-pairing values, duplicating, fabricating, and replacing cases) are applied to three common tests: the independent *t*-test, Pearson *r* correlation, and the Chi-square test for a 2x2 contingency table. Results demonstrate that, in small samples, only a small absolute number of tampers are typically needed to obtain significant results. In large samples, although the absolute number of tampers needed grows, the proportion of the sample needing to be tampered with to obtain significance falls rapidly. The strategies that alter no recorded value, and so are plausibly hardest to detect, are among the most effective. Critically, unjustifiably deleting inconvenient data points, which researchers rate as far more defensible than invention, is no less dangerous than outright fabrication: both manufacture false positives from null data reliably, and at comparable and very small cost (e.g., median tampers of 5-10% at moderate sample sizes across tests). Fabricating and falsifying results therefore requires a worryingly small amount of actual data tampering.

title: Emoticon variation: Noses and rotations do not alter meaning, but mouths and mirrorings do
description: Emoticons can visually differ in various minor ways. This includes presence or absence of an element, like the 'nose' or 'tear' in the :-) and :'( emoticons, differences in orientation, as in the :) versus (: emoticons, or a change to an element, such as the 'eyes' in the :) versus ;) emoticons. It is unclear which types of variation impact meaning or whether there is consistency in the types of variation that have the most effect on meaning. We present a study investigating how emoticon variations are perceived and interpreted in a range of contexts, including positive, negative, and sarcastic. Given that an established function of emoticons is to clarify message intent, and research suggests non-native speakers may use emoticons in a compensatory way, we also compare the perceptions and interpretations of native (n = 151) and non-native (n = 119) speakers of English in each context type. Utilising emoticons that were produced by participants in earlier research, a series of ratings and emoticon selections reveal patterns of contextual use, interpretation, and perceptions of meaning equivalence. Results reveal that specific visual variations, including the nose element or rotation of an emoticon, have little impact on meaning, while other variations, such as mouthshape or mirroring an emoticon, do alter meaning. The scale of visual change does not correlate with meaning change. Results also indicate native and non-native speakers pattern very closely in their overall use and interpretation, suggesting emoticons can be useful in facilitating cross-cultural or cross-linguistic conversations. However, there are important exceptions with more subtle emoticon variations and in more semantically complex contexts. This suggests the nuances of emoticon usage within a language community take more time to acquire.

title: A guide to evaluating LLM-based extraction and judgement tools
description: Researchers have begun to delegate extraction and judgement research tasks to tools built on large language models (LLMs), including the annotation of text, screening of papers, extraction of numerical values, and identification of supporting passages. Existing guidance establishes that these tools should be validated, documented, and tested for robustness. Researchers still need practical guidance, however, on how precisely different tools can be most appropriately evaluated. This paper provides a step-by-step workflow for evaluating such tools. This involves firstly defining the tool’s output, identifying the desired comparator, and specifying what would count as satisfactory performance – from these decisions, the appropriate analyses and requirements for comparison can be determined and conducted. I provide a worked example of this evaluation approach based on a simulated systematic review extraction-and-judgement tool.

title: Human or AI? An Interpretable Method for Auditing  Free-Text Data in Online Psychological Research
description: Online psychological studies increasingly rely on free-text responses, but the availability of generative AI creates new challenges for evaluating the authenticity and integrity of data pertaining to human introspection. We present an interpretable text-analysis workflow for identifying linguistic cues associated with perceived AI authorship in digital journal entries. Across a two-week journalling study, 251 participants submitted 2,808 text entries, which were independently labelled by human annotators as human-written, AI-generated or invalid, and compared with classifications from a commercial AI-detection tool. We extracted 127 transparent features capturing length, semantic coherence, stylistic consistency, readability, natural-language-inference-based consistency, lexical overlap and Linguistic Inquiry Word Count 2022 psycholinguistic categories. On a high-confidence subset defined by convergence between human judgements and automated detection, interpretable classifiers strongly distinguished entries perceived as human from those perceived as AI-generated. A decision tree achieved 95.3% accuracy using a small set of auditable rules based on verb rate, syllable count, article use and sentence count, while a linear SVM identified 18.6% of entries as ambiguous cases suitable for human review. Entries perceived as AI-generated were longer, more coherent, more stylistically uniform and more formally structured, whereas entries perceived as human showed greater present focus, self-reference and stylistic variability. These findings provide a transparent framework for auditing possible AI mediation in remote psychological text data, while showing how interpretable models can support human review rather than replace it.

title: Brief and simultaneous assessment of delay, probability, and joint delay–probability discounting: Initial validation of the three-for-one discounting task in tobacco use [preprint]
description:
Abstract
While delay discounting (DD) is a reliable marker of tobacco use, far less is known about probability discounting (PD) or how delay and risk jointly influence decision-making. To allow simultaneous assessment of DD, PD, and their interaction, we developed the three-for-one (TFO) discounting task. In 36 trials (<3 minutes), the TFO task estimates Effective Delay 50 (ED50) across a range of reward probabilities, allowing both empirical analysis of how risk impacts DD and quantitative modeling to derive independent DD and PD rates (k, h). Adults (n=134) reporting current- or never-cigarette smoking completed the TFO task, standalone DD and PD tasks, and a risk-numeracy scale (measuring understanding of risk/probability). The current vs. never-smoking group showed lower ED50 (higher DD) for certain/near-certain rewards (ps≤.021), but not riskier rewards. TFO-derived DD and PD rates showed evidence of known-groups validity (sensitivity to smoking-related DD differences, p=.002), discriminant validity (small correlation between DD and PD, r=.11), and convergent validity (moderate-to-strong correspondence with standalone tasks, ps<.001). The never-smoking group showed higher between-task correspondence in DD (p=.001); however, this effect was better accounted for by a moderating role of risk numeracy, evident in both DD and PD (ps<.001). Collectively, the TFO task showed that risk attenuates smoking-related group differences in DD and provided generally accurate assessment of DD and PD rates. Accuracy may be lower in participants with lower risk numeracy, but this does not impact sensitivity to known group differences in DD. Future work should explore additional validation approaches while evaluating methods to mitigate numeracy-related effects.

title: Unpacking Human Decision Strategies during AI-aided Decision-making
description: Interventions aimed at improving appropriate reliance on AI have had mixed effectiveness. We argue that this may be due to the lack of attention to individual differences in human decision strategies, combined with overconfidence in relying on the results of aggregate-level analyses. We approach this issue in a set of three studies. In Study 1, we design a set of decision strategies grounded in self- and AI-confidence to provide a robust first-order approximation of what individual strategies can be. We use simulation to assess the conditions under which these strategies are identifiable. In Study 2, using a face-matching task, we measured whether participants adjusted their initial decisions when an AI model advised the opposite response with varying levels of confidence. Group-level analyses suggest that both initial self-confidence and AI confidence are strong predictors of human reliance on AI advice. However, when assessing the strategies at the individual level, we find evidence for the fact that a sizable subset of participants did not attend to both confidence scores, contradicting the group-level analyses. Using simulation (Study 3), we show that group-level analyses can easily paint a picture of the underlying strategies that is at odds with the actual underlying distribution of individual strategies. Taken together, our results underscore the critical role of recognizing individual human decision strategies in dealing with AI to better understand and support human-AI decision-making.

title: Culture shapes cognition and motives in early social interactions
description: In this study, we test the hypothesis that culture shapes cognition and motives in early social interactions. Infants from Ibadan (Nigeria, n = 66, M = 2.2 years, SD = 0.2) and Regensburg (Germany, n = 49, M = 2.3 years, SD = 0.2) were instructed to hand over three objects in two culture-specific ways, by imperatives (e.g., “Give the spoon to me, now!”), being typical for Ibadan, and by requests (e.g., “Could you give me the shoe, please?”), being typical for Regensburg. We found a cultural congruency effect: infants in Ibadan were more responsive to imperatives and infants in Regensburg were more responsive to requests. This response pattern was explained by cross-cultural differences in maternal scaffolding when assigning a task to their infant, which was more assertive (i.e., direct prompts) in Ibadan and more deliberate (i.e., kind requests) in Regensburg. Critically, infants showed higher levels of confusion and protest when confronted with culturally incongruent prompts, unveiling culturally adjusted cognition and motives underlying their response tendencies. These findings highlight the primary role of culturally adjusted parent-child interactions in regulating infants’ social behaviors along culture-specific attractor-states.

title: Building Science Identity Through University-High School Partnerships: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of a Graduate Student-Led Science Expo
description: Research-practice partnerships provide a promising framework for designing and evaluating STEM outreach, yet the role of graduate student organizations as sustained research partners remains underexplored. We examined a graduate-student-led partnership (a science exposition) between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a local high school aimed at fostering science identity in highschoolers from historically underrepresented backgrounds. Quantitative analyses (N = 48) showed pre-to-post-expo increases in overall science identity, with significant gains in perceived representation and recognition as a science person. Qualitative analyses (N = 64) of open-ended post-reflection questions highlighted the importance of interacting with relatable researchers, authentic scientific engagement, and representation. These findings illustrate how graduate student organizations can function as research-practice partners by integrating outreach, evaluation, and continuous improvement.

title: The developmental dynamics of bilingual spelling:  Longitudinal and intervention evidence for language-specific orthographic differentiation
description: Spelling in bilingual children requires navigating two orthographic systems that may compete as well as cooperate. Although bilingual language research demonstrates extensive cross-language co-activation, far less is known about how such dynamics shape spelling development. We investigated whether cross-linguistic influence in spelling – indexed by the extent to which children’s misspellings conformed to English-consistent versus Welsh-consistent phoneme–grapheme mappings – predicted literacy development in Welsh–English bilingual children. Across three studies involving 524 children aged approximately 7–11 years, we quantified the extent to which misspellings reflected sublexical mappings characteristic of English or Welsh orthography. In Study 1, longitudinal analyses of children in control groups showed that greater phonological plausibility under English-consistent mappings at baseline predicted greater growth in English spelling accuracy, whereas greater plausibility under Welsh-consistent mappings predicted slower growth. In Study 2, a Welsh-medium literacy intervention did not affect English spelling accuracy but strengthened Welsh-consistent mappings and improved English-consistent mappings among children with the weakest baseline skills. In Study 3, an English-medium intervention strengthened English-consistent mappings but did not alter Welsh-consistent mappings. Together, these findings suggest that bilingual spelling development involves increasing differentiation of language-specific sublexical mappings through experience. This differentiation appears to be shaped by instructional context and orthographic depth, such that increasing sensitivity to target-language mappings supports spelling growth, whereas persistent influence of non-target mappings may constrain it.

title: Functional Brain Activation during Statistical Learning is Related to Rapid Automatized Naming of Digits and Objects (but not Letters): An fMRI Study
description:
Purpose: Statistical learning (SL) is the implicit process of extracting statistical regularities from the environment and has been found to be strongly linked with language ability in both children and adults. Notably, SL has been shown to activate brain regions that are implicated in language/reading; however, the extent to which this brain activity is related to reading-related tasks is unknown. Here, we used fMRI to explore the brain-behavior relationships between SL and reading processes.
Methods: 48 Adult participants (28 Female, mean age 21 years old) completed a Visual SL (VSL) task inside the MRI that included two phases: 1) familiarization, wherein participants were presented with novel triplets of shapes varying in transitional probabilities, and 2) testing, which involved selecting best-fitting triplets that assessed their learning of these probabilities. Outside the scanner, participants completed three Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) tasks consisting of quickly naming strings of digits, letters, and objects as a measure of basic reading ability.
Results: Using a whole-brain correlational approach with RAN performance as covariates, significant brain-behavior clusters were identified between VSL task-evoked neural activity with RAN digits and objects, but not letters. The regions were predominantly left-lateralized in visuospatial-motor network as well as the parietal regions, caudate, and cerebellum, with the precuneus as a common hub.
Conclusion: These findings link to a more multimodal understanding of the neurocognitive processes, indicating that SL-related neural activity in skilled readers is preferentially linked to naming of symbol sets with inherent semantic content (digits, objects) rather than arbitrary orthographic forms (letters).

title: The Role of Temperament and Personality Traits in the Development of ADHD from Late Childhood through Adolescence
description: Individual differences in temperament and personality traits may shed light on the presentation and development of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across adolescence. The present study used multi-method, longitudinal data from a large sample of Mexican-origin youth (N = 674; 50% girls) to examine associations between ADHD symptoms (including combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive subtypes) and a wide range of temperament and personality traits assessed via self-, mother-, and father-reports and coded observational data. First, we found moderate one-year rank-order stabilities of combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive ADHD symptoms (r’s ranging from .27 to .51), but relatively low eight-year rank-order stability from age 10 to 17 (r = .19 for combined); eight-year stability was higher for boys than girls. Second, hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms were both negatively correlated with concurrent effortful control and conscientiousness, and positively correlated with impulsivity, negative emotionality, and neuroticism; in addition, hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were positively associated with surgency and extraversion. Third, bivariate latent growth curve models showed that the levels and slopes of effortful control (and its facets) and negative emotionality (particularly the frustration, aggression, and depressed mood facets) were significantly related to the levels and slopes of ADHD symptom trajectories. Findings from random-intercept cross-lagged panel models showed that temperament domains and ADHD symptoms had meaningful between- and within-person associations, but no significant cross-lagged associations. Associations were stronger for adolescent self-reports of temperament/personality than for mother reports. Overall, findings highlight connections between temperament and personality traits with ADHD symptoms across adolescence.

title: Two temporally distinct prediction stages overlap under moderately faster speech
description: Prediction is a core mechanism in language comprehension, and evidence suggests it involves separate stages. The associative stage involves fast, automatic predictions driven by semantic associations (e.g., a verb cueing likely referents), while the strategic stage involves slower, deliberate predictions incorporating broader contextual cues (e.g., agent gender). Although faster speech has been shown to decrease prediction, no research has investigated how these stages are individually impacted. We conducted a preregistered visual-world eye-tracking experiment in which English speakers listened to non-speeded (4 syllables/second) or speeded (5.5 syllables/second) sentences while viewing four-object arrays. Stimuli included a female or male agent (Kate or James) and a verb (e.g., wear) that primed two target images (e.g., dress and tie) alongside two unrelated distractor images (e.g., hairdryer and drill). Verb-related targets included one stereotypically compatible with the agent’s gender and one incompatible. One distractor was gender-compatible and one gender-incompatible. Participants showed associative predictions (more fixations to verb-related targets than distractors) and strategic predictions (more fixations to agent-compatible targets than incompatible targets). In non-speeded speech, the stages were temporally distinct, with associative prediction occurring before strategic prediction. In speeded speech, however, these stages overlapped. These results suggest that changes in speech rate can influence predictive timing.

title: Multilevel Reward Prediction Errors Drive Emotional Valence During Perceptual Decision-Making
description: What role do expectations, outcomes, and their mismatches—i.e., reward prediction errors (RPEs)—play in generating emotions? Existing theories make competing predictions, with value-based perspectives suggesting that emotional valence tracks the value of outcomes and expectations, value-updating perspectives suggesting that it instead tracks RPEs, a common value-learning signal, and mixed views suggesting a role for all three factors. Yet empirical tests of these predictions have produced mixed results. Here, we demonstrate how these conflicting results could be explained within a value-updating perspective, as resulting from multiple simultaneous RPEs operating at different levels and timescales. In particular, we build off recent work which suggested that affect in a perceptual decision-making task was influenced by both expectations and outcomes, but not by RPEs. The current study re-evaluates this conclusion, by modifying the original task and analyses to dissociate trial-level and block-level RPEs through their unique temporal dynamics. Results showed that both forms of RPEs drove affect in this task, with no clear effect of expectations or outcomes beyond this, contrary to previous conclusions. These results thus support value-updating perspectives, while highlighting the importance of considering multiple forms of RPEs when accounting for affective valence. Moreover, demonstrating key links between value-updating signals and emotions has broad implications for affective science.

title: When and why stimulus repetition does not lead to learning
description: Three experiments investigated absence and presence of learning from multiple repeated presentations. Typically, recall of a verbal list or visual array improves with as few as six repetitions of the same stimulus. However, recognition paradigms have shown no learning with 60 or more repetitions of the same stimulus. Ye et al. (2026) reported no performance improvements and no awareness of repetition across 120 repetition trials with a 500 ms study-test interval for change detection. With longer study-test intervals only some participants improved performance. We explored whether lack of learning arose from short study-test intervals, or forgetting during longer inter-trial intervals. General working memory capacity (OSPAN) was assessed for each participant. Study-test, not inter-trial, intervals modulated absence or presence of learning and repetition awareness. OSPAN correlated with performance only when learning was observed. These new results highlight the importance of strategy differences in how participants perform cognitive tasks, that are not apparent in aggregate group data. Results also are consistent with the Ye et al. (2026; Logie, 1995; Shimi & Logie, 2019) proposal that lack of learning across repetitions reflects a temporary visual cache memory within a trial, the contents of which are over-written by the array on the next trial, even if arrays are identical. A weak episodic memory is formed but cannot support performance unless cumulative strengthening across trials reaches a threshold for observable learning. General working memory capacity for encoding and retrieval is engaged only if participants show learning and awareness of the array repetition.

title: Seeing Beyond Replication Success: A Framework for Evaluating Multi-Lab Replication Outcomes Using Meta-Analytic Bayes Factors
description: This study introduces a new replication success classification framework for multi-lab replication studies that goes beyond the traditional binary distinction of replication success and failure. The framework distinguishes between true and false replication successes and failures, revealing the underlying composition of observed replication results and how they are shaped by study-level factors in both the original and replication studies. Using a large-scale simulation, we evaluated four meta-analytic Bayes factor (MABF) methods as tools for determining replication success within this framework. Results showed that the MABF methods were generally more effective at ruling out spurious effects than at confirming small true effects. The one-sided fixed-effect meta-analytic Bayes factor and the inclusion Bayes factor methods most reliably identified genuine replication success. The framework illustrates how bias and methodological choices influence the underlying composition of replication outcomes. These findings provide a more nuanced understanding of replication results and offer practical guidance for designing and evaluating future large-scale replication projects to strengthen research reproducibility.

title: Statistical learning generalizes across phonological context and transfers to vowel production
description: Recent experience rapidly shapes speech perception, but whether this learning influences speech production remains a central question for sensorimotor theories of speech. Prior work has shown that dimension-based statistical learning can transfer from perception to production for consonants. The present research tested whether this transfer extends to vowels and to vowel duration, a temporal dimension whose role in speech motor control is not fully specified in current models. Across four experiments, listeners were passively exposed to short-term distributional regularities that either preserved or reversed the typical English relationship between spectral quality and duration for /æ/–/ɛ/ vowels. Exposure to the reversed regularity reduced listeners’ reliance on duration in vowel categorization and reduced durational differentiation in their own vowel productions. These perception–production effects replicated across four experiments. Experiments 2–4 further showed that learning generalized beyond the exposure context to novel phonological environments that varied in coda, onset–coda context, and segmental structure, and that this generalized learning also transferred to production. The findings indicate that statistical regularities in others’ speech can dynamically reshape the weighting of temporal information in both vowel perception and production, placing new constraints on sensorimotor accounts of speech learning and control.

title: Large Language Models Reveal the Content and Consistency of Suicidal Thoughts: A Two- Study Longitudinal Investigation Among Adolescents and Young Adults
description: Suicide is a leading cause of death. Measurement of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) relies on self-report (e.g., “How strong is your urge to kill yourself right now?”), yet little is known about how individuals translate internal experiences into numerical ratings. We used large language models (LLMs) to examine the content and consistency of suicide urges across severity ratings, between people, and over time. Participants with past-year STBs (Study 1: N=158 adolescents, Study 2: N=202 young adults) completed open-ended questions at baseline and follow-ups. We developed a two-stage topic-modeling pipeline and identified 13 (Study 1) and 14 (Study 2) topics reflecting suicidal thought content (e.g., Family/Friends Reactions, Depressed & Exhausted). Within- and between-person consistency were U-shaped, with highest agreement at endpoints of the scale. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs for advancing measurement of suicide risk and our understanding of how people interpret and respond to self-report rating scales.

title: Cracking the multidimensionality of cognition with cross-domain transfer
description: Higher-order cognition emerges from the interaction of multiple cognitive processes, yet these processes remain difficult to measure during ongoing task performance. Recent work across humans, non-human animals, and artificial neural networks suggests that cognition is compositional and that cognitive processes are represented by abstract, reusable neural representations that generalize across tasks. These findings show that it is possible to decode neural signatures of a specific cognitive process in one task and covertly track its engagement in another, an approach we term cross-domain transfer. Here, we argue that cross-domain transfer provides a unifying framework for studying cognition as a system of reusable cognitive processes. We place cross-domain transfer within the broader evolution of cognitive decoding methods, discuss its theoretical foundations, and synthesize emerging evidence across cognitive domains. This framework provides new opportunities to test mechanistic theories of cognition and develop more interpretable, process-level approaches for real-time cognitive monitoring and intervention.

title: Investigating the effect of text appearance on visual search for typos
description:
We engage in visual search in many daily activities, from hunting for keys to scanning
a grocery list for missed items. A subset of these search tasks (e.g., looking through a grocery
list) additionally intersect with the process of reading, requiring the observer to recognize text as
they search for a target. In these settings, how do manipulations of text appearance, which
normally affect reading performance, affect the visual search process? The present study uses a
modified version of a real-world visual search task, typo detection, to examine how stimulus font
impacts performance. One possibility is that hard-to-read fonts could hinder typo detection by
either impeding word identification or shifting quitting thresholds. Alternatively, hard-to-read
fonts could, counterintuitively, facilitate typo detection by slowing the reader down and requiring
more effortful processing. Across two different experiments, participants searched for typos in
blocks of text that varied in stroke contrast (Experiment 1) and letter width (Experiment 2).
Across both experiments, font did not impact accuracy, but participants were slower to respond
after fixating typos written in hard- versus easy-to-read fonts. Hierarchical drift diffusion
modelling isolated the mechanism underlying this difference: in Experiment 2, the rate of
evidence accumulation was significantly lower for hard- versus easy-to-read trials, while non-
decision time and decision threshold were unimpacted. These findings reveal that, though one’s
typo detection performance may be robust to changes in text appearance, there are subtle
differences in the rate of processing stimuli that impact the time course of target identification.

title: Music was my first love: Biographic resonance makes everyday music listening meaningful
description: Despite much research on eudaimonic media experiences, little is known about how and why certain content is perceived as meaningful by certain users in certain situations. We therefore examine biographic resonance — connections between entertainment content and users’ biographic memories — during everyday music listening on Spotify and propose that memory recall, as well as its emotional valence, relate to meaningfulness via distinct patterns of intrinsic need satisfaction. Results from a preregistered, intensive-longitudinal study (144 persons; 6,920 situations) reveal that biographic resonance relates to both high- and low-effort modes of eudaimonic entertainment. Moreover, by linking users’ self-reports with their tracked digital music use (2,786 sessions; 107,147 songs), we find that the occurrence and quality of biographic resonance vary across situations and are shaped by both content and contextual factors within algorithmically curated environments. Our results highlight how resonances between media users’ selves and entertainment content foster situational meaningfulness in everyday life.

title: Effect-Based Assessments of Intergroup Comparability  – The Practical Impact of Measurement Non-Invariance & Differential Item Functioning on Psychological Tests and Scales
description: To assess psychological tests and scales for violations of intergroup comparability – termed Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) in factor analysis and Differential Item Functioning (DIF) in item response theory – statistical testing has emerged as the dominating approach, but inherently fails to differentiate between major and negligible violations. To address this, upwards of 27 effect size measures for both MNI and DIF have been proposed over the last decades, using vastly different conventions in naming and notation, with no clear consensus on interpretation. This arguably constitutes a severe hindrance for the much needed popularization of a non-dichotomous assessments of intergroup comparability. We address this limitation by introducing a unifying taxonomy that encompasses all previous measures as instances of just four fundamental types: Expected Difference (ED), Expected Absolute Difference (EAD), Total Expected Difference (TED) and Total Expected Absolute Difference (TEAD), which are universally applicable, irrespective of the underlying measurement model. Furthermore, we construct corresponding effect directions and derive formulas to calulate MNI/DIF-induced biases in commonly used mean difference effects, such as Cohen’s d & Cohen’s f. We provide a dual illustration using both FA and IRT models on real-world data.

title: Effects of a Neuroticism Intervention Over One Year
description:
Introduction: Personality interventions recently gained increasing interest as promising tools to improve people’s lives. Although initial evidence on the effects of these interventions is promising, their longer-term effectiveness has yet to be established. 
Methods: Using data form the Changing How I Live Life (CHILL) Study, we examined the effects of a digital neuroticism intervention over 1 year. In this study, participants (N = 475) were randomized to an active control group or intervention groups targeting different levels of neuroticism. Furthermore, participants reported on different aspects of perceived intervention utility at the 1-year follow-up. 
Results: Participants significantly decreased in their neuroticism from pre-intervention to the 1-year follow-up regardless of whether they were randomized to the intervention groups (d = -0.40 to -0.53) or the active control group (d = -0.41). Intervention effects did also not differ among groups targeting different levels of neuroticism. Nonetheless, participants were relatively happy with the intervention and reported a high willingness to pay money to get access to a similar app. 
Conclusion: This study provides novel insights into the durability of intervention-induced neuroticism changes, but future research is needed to better understand the mechanisms and boundary conditions of volitional personality changes with and without interventions.

title: The Role of Individual Differences in the Effects of PC and VR Simulations on Elementary School Students’ Learning and Curiosity
description: Curiosity is related to important academic outcomes. Yet, current research suggests that children’s curiosity decreases during formal schooling, and research exploring theory-informed interventions to increase curiosity remains limited. Building on a synthesis of prior research, the SIM-Curious framework is introduced, identifying pathways to support curiosity-driven learning with simulations. Then, results of a pre-registered, randomized field trial (N = 217, Mage = 13.22 years, SD = 0.94) are presented, examining the overall effects of simulations and the relative effects of media (Virtual Reality vs PCs) in promoting curiosity and knowledge. Students’ specific state curiosity and knowledge increased, but there were no significant main effects of media. Higher prior specific state curiosity indirectly influenced follow-up knowledge through question-asking during the simulation. Individual differences in trait curiosity, prior knowledge, in-simulation question-asking, and post-simulation specific state curiosity influenced post-intervention information-seeking. The results are discussed in light of the SIM-Curious framework and illustrate its promise.

title: The Sensitivity of Rasch Tree DIF Detection to Model Misspecification
description: The Rasch Tree model for differential item functioning (DIF) detection is a useful tool that uses exploratory yet interpretable methods to investigate intersectional DIF. Recent research has explored Rasch Tree performance under specific data conditions. The present research expands upon this by examining the effect of Rasch model misspecifications (i.e., misfit) on Rasch Tree estimation performance. Using a Monte Carlo simulation, we test the effects of including discrimination and pseudo-guessing parameters in the data generation process on DIF detection accuracy, DIF magnitude estimates, and resulting Rasch Tree structure. Results indicate that imposing the Rasch model on data that contain varied item discriminations and guessing behavior leads to a decrease in DIF detection accuracy and stability. In addition, we also assess these effects under different sample sizes and test lengths and examine the Rasch Tree’s ability to distinguish between person ability differences and item level DIF under various conditions.  We discuss implications and future directions from this research.

title: Recovery order in adaptive systems is set by dependency structure
description: Adaptive systems recover their capacities in reproducible orders. Predicting it has meant fitting a dynamical model to each system and reading the order off its trajectories, an output of the fit, not of structure. Here we show that recovery order follows from dependency structure: which capacities must be in place before which others recover. From four axioms we prove that where prerequisite gates vanish at baseline no capacity begins to recover before its prerequisites, whatever the rate constants, and that under a common deficit-closing rule with rates non-increasing along dependencies the admissible orders are exactly the linear extensions of the graph: a chain gives a unique sequence, a branch a partial order. We map where steep heterogeneity adds further orders. The graph is an input, realized in probabilistic models as identifiability structure. We instantiate it in catatonia, post-injury motor recovery and curriculum learning, the last without a probabilistic model.

title: Stimulated recall protocols: Field-specific guidelines for second language acquisition and bilingualism research
description: Stimulated recall protocols are one of the most popular methods in second language acquisition and bilingualism research to investigate language learners’ internal thought processes when using second languages. Although methodological handbooks are available for learning how to set up a stimulated recall study, there is little empirically driven guidance on best practices for reporting variables central to the method. To develop field-specific reporting guidelines, this systematic review analyzed articles that used stimulated recall to elicit introspective reports in sixteen Q1 journals in applied linguistics between 2000 and 2024. After screening, 171 studies were analyzed for 62 variables inherent to this practice. Findings showed that some details were well-reported, but others critical for stimulated recalls, such as the use of instructions or the L2 proficiency of participants, were reported infrequently. The review concludes with empirically derived reporting guidelines derived from the literature to support authors, editors, and peer reviewers.

title: Pupil size dynamics predict momentary changes in self-reported arousal
description: Subjective arousal, or feelings of activation and alertness, can dynamically modulate affect, behavior, and cognition. Momentary changes in subjective arousal have typically been assessed with self-report in humans, which may alter those very feelings. Although researchers have traditionally used pupil size as a physiological index of arousal, links between pupil dynamics and momentary changes in subjective arousal remain unclear. Here, we combined continuous pupillometry with repeated self-report probes of changing arousal as individuals engaged in a modified Monetary Incentive Delay task. Across Virtual Reality (N = 28; 12 females, 16 males) and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (N = 27; 15 females, 12 males) studies, tonic and phasic pupil measures jointly predicted subsequent self-reported arousal beyond stated incentive value and at a temporal lag of approximately 1.5–3.5 seconds. Neural activity associated with pupil dynamics further predicted pupil size, self-reported arousal, and behavioral motivation in held-out data. Together, these convergent findings establish pupil size as a temporally-precise marker of momentary fluctuations in self-reported arousal.

title: Imagination boosts strategy learning
description: Imagination is thought to boost exploration and problem solving by simulating states that have not been directly experienced as a means of reasoning through future plans. Here we tested this idea in the context of an impartial combinatorial game with a ground truth optional strategy. Adopting a stumbler-strategist reinforcement learning architecture, we showed how imagination can boost optimal strategy learning over memory replay. These model predictions were validated experimentally in humans (N=255) using an intervention design where participants were tasked with either imagining unplayed scenarios, reviewing prior games, or engaging in a simple visual attention task (control). These convergent results show how imagination uniquely boosts strategy learning in partially explored tasks.

title: Bilingual experience predicts language skills, but not reading skills, in a low-literacy and multilingual context
description: Children throughout the world attend school and learn to read in a language of instruction (LoI) other than the language(s) they speak at home, which is one factor contributing to poor reading outcomes. Understanding reading development in multilingual, Majority World contexts is important for improving reading skills globally. In a linguistically diverse sample of children in rural Côte d’Ivoire, we examined how home language experience (monolingual, regional bilingual [two Ivorian languages], French bilingual [French + Ivorian language], French multilingual [French + two Ivorian languages]) relates to children’s (N = 1335) language and reading skills. Bilingual children (French and regional) outperformed monolingual children on French language tasks, suggesting bilingual experience benefits language skills regardless of whether it includes the LoI (French). However, this language advantage did not extend to reading; there were no differences in reading scores between groups and all children leveraged phonological awareness for reading regardless of their home language experience. The findings suggest that bilingual/multilingual education programs, and reading instruction that strengthens language skills, may support reading outcomes in multilingual, Majority World contexts.

title: Welcome to the Jangle (Fallacy): The Case of Statistics and Mathematics Anxieties
description:
Background: Statistics-related anxiety is a common barrier to learning in higher education, particularly for psychology and other non-specialist students. High prevalence rates are concerning because statistical literacy is integral to academic success, employability, and informed citizenship. Clarifying the nature of statistics anxiety is central to understanding it, yet it remains unclear whether statistics anxiety is genuinely distinct from mathematics anxiety or simply another manifestation of the same construct.

Aims: We examined the degree of overlap (jangle fallacy) between the Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS) and the Revised Mathematics Anxiety Rating Scale (R-MARS).

Samples: Two cohorts of UK undergraduate psychology students participated: Study 1 (n = 489) and Study 2 (n = 245).

Methods: Each study combined a cross-sectional survey with a between-participants experiment. Surveys included the STARS, R-MARS, parallel forms to control for scale content, and measures of trait and state anxiety. In the experiment, participants were randomly assigned to complete either a statistics or mathematics multiple-choice test, with state anxiety measured before and after.

Results:
Results pointed to overlap across all analyses and samples. Scales were highly correlated, items did not separate into distinct domains, individuals rarely reported one without the other, and state anxiety increased similarly across test types.

Conclusions:
Findings show that statistics anxiety, as measured by the STARS, is not distinct from mathematics anxiety, as measured by the R-MARS. Recognising statistics anxiety as part of the broader mathematics anxiety construct can streamline measurement, clarify theory, and support more effective interventions for reducing quantitative anxieties in education.

title: How we see relations: the case of containment and support
description: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography (EEG) on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens (“in” or “on”) but rather as objects’ properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning.

title: The crossword effect: A recall advantage for words encoded in alignment with their spatial associations
description: Across two preregistered experiments, we demonstrate that free word recall improves when words are encoded in alignment with their spatial associations. Experiment 1 compared words with a strong horizontal association (e.g., railway) to words with a strong vertical association (e.g., rocket) and established that the latter were more likely to be recalled when presented vertically rather than horizontally during encoding. No such benefit was observed for horizontally associated words. Experiment 2 extended these findings by showing a vertical encoding advantage also for spatially neutral words (e.g., foam), which was smaller than for the vertically associated words but larger than for the horizontally associated words in Experiment 1. Beyond suggesting a general vertical encoding advantage in free word recall, the results support Barsalou's (1999) Perceptual Symbol Hypothesis, which posits that word meanings are grounded in perception and action. Our findings demonstrate that access to word concepts in short term memory is modulated by sensorimotor processes during encoding, specifically horizontal versus vertical reading.

title: Growth Trajectory Profiles of Self-concept of Abilities, Intrinsic Value, Utility Value, and Emotional Cost in Math Across Grades 4 to 8
description:
Background: Previous research has consistently shown that students’ math motivation declines across the school years. However, less is known about individual differences in these developmental trajectories. 
Aim: This study investigated the development of students’ math self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, utility value and emotional cost from Grades 4 to 8 at the average level and by identifying distinct growth trajectory profiles. Profile membership was further related to gender and performance. 
Sample: The sample comprised 875 Finnish students (53 % girls) from Grades 4 to 8 using an accelerated longitudinal design. 
Method: Latent growth curve models and growth mixture modeling were utilized. Gender differences were analyzed using the 3-step approach and differences in math performance were examined using the BCH method.
Results: On average, self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, and utility value declined whereas emotional cost increased over time. Three trajectory profiles were identified: Positive declining reflected the normative developmental pattern, while students in the Struggling profile showed lower initial motivation, increasing emotional cost, and the lowest math performance. Further, students in the Fading interest profile, predominantly boys, maintained high self-concept and performance despite low/moderate utility value and steeply declining intrinsic value. 
Conclusion: The average developmental trends concealed individual differences in students’ motivational development. While most students followed the expected decline, distinct profiles showed that motivation can develop differently across students and have different implications for academic performance.

title: Identifying Acoustic Characteristics for Disgust-Related Musical Stimuli
description: Disgust remains one of the least studied emotions in music psychology, largely because music is typically regarded as an aesthetic medium and because disgust is phylogenetically rooted in chemical and tactile rather than auditory senses. This study addresses the absence of standardized musical stimuli for disgust through two sequential experiments involving the affective evaluation of 36 musical clips (20 s each) composed to represent three categories: disgust, positive, and neutral. In Experiment 1 (n = 125), participants rated the clips on valence, arousal, and a disgust–fear continuum. Disgust clips occupied the low-valence, high-arousal quadrant but were not consistently differentiated from fear. Seven clips were revised by removing low-register pedals, increasing the salience of sounds semantically associated with contamination, and reducing rhythmic regularity. In Experiment 2 (n = 62), the revised clips achieved significant differentiation from fear on the continuum. Results suggest that musical expression of disgust requires not merely abstract structural codes but the integration of indexical sounds associated with contamination experiences within non-tonal musical environments. These findings provide a methodological foundation for constructing disgust-related auditory stimuli applicable to research on music-evoked emotions and their interaction with moral and political judgment.

title: Some psycholinguistic effect sizes are larger in the lab than on web-based platforms
description: The increasing use of web-based platforms for evaluating quantitative predictions in psycholinguistics raises an important methodological question: are effect sizes estimated on these platforms comparable to those obtained in laboratory settings? To address this question, we replicated an existing self-paced reading study designed to measure garden-path and syntactic adaptation effects across four platforms: SONA-lab, SONA-online, Prolific, and MTurk. We found that garden-path effects were consistently larger in the laboratory than on all three web-based platforms. Exploratory analyses of filler items revealed a similar attenuation of word frequency and word position effects in the web-based platforms. Together, these findings suggest that testing platform can systematically influence estimated effect sizes and should therefore be considered when evaluating quantitative predictions in psycholinguistics.

title: Illusion of control, gambler’s fallacy, or neither? Testing key models of gambling psychology by extending Langer and Roth (1975)
description: Cognitive biases about randomness, such as the illusion of control and the gambler’s fallacy, are central to the widely-used cognitive models of disordered gambling. In a highly-cited foundational paper, Langer and Roth (1975) found that participants thought they were better at predicting coin-flips when they were randomised to receive more wins at the start rather than the end of a 30-flip sequence. This replicable effect, which has been attributed to the illusion of control, could also be driven by biases that do not involve active involvement, such as the gambler’s fallacy. We therefore designed a large-scale (N=1,594) online 2x2 experiment, where the sequence manipulation was crossed with a manipulation of active involvement, with “self” participants dictating the coin-flips personally, and “other” participants viewing another participant’s flips and predictions. The original effect of sequence replicated, occurring across both “self” and “other” conditions.
